Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips.
  • Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem.
  • Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This indicates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an vital step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This indicates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an vital step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors.

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Industry observers note that microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

Sources indicate that this effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%.

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

In a recent development, the team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the latest technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error.".

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors.

Recent findings suggest that the findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

It has been revealed that this is especially notable for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

According to recent reports, "By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," states Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.".

Industry observers note that the broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TSMC declared at its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop this week that its A14 (1.4nm-class) fabrication technology is ready for customer design work and version 0.9 of its process design kit (PDK) is ready.
  • "A14 0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design in," a TSMC spokesman noted on stage at the 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop.
  • According to recent reports, A14 uses TSMC's 2nd Generation nanosheet transistors and its NanoFlex Pro standard cell architecture, which supports Boost Cells to enable higher performance as well as Low-Power Cells to reduce power consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TSMC declared at its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop this week that its A14 (1.4nm-class) fabrication technology is ready for customer design work and version 0.9 of its process design kit (PDK) is ready. TSMC also detailed Boost Cells, a way for the newly introduced node to deliver 14% higher performance compared to N2P, and how customers can migrate their designs to A13 in the future. Furthermore, Cadence and Synopsys have both completed full design-flow certification on an Arm Cortex-A725 CPU core, which gives chip designers two validated toolchains to build their 14A chips.

"A14 0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design in," a TSMC spokesman noted on stage at the 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop.

According to recent reports, A14 uses TSMC's 2nd Generation nanosheet transistors and its NanoFlex Pro standard cell architecture, which supports Boost Cells to enable higher performance as well as Low-Power Cells to reduce power consumption. Designers can place compact high-speed Boost Cells on critical paths (which resembles Intel's Turbo Cells supported by its 14A fabrication technology) and use Low-Power Cells with narrower nanosheets for general logic or parts of the chip that do not need high performance.

In a recent development, in general, TSMC promises A14 with NanoFlex Pro optimizations to deliver a 14% speed gain at the same power or a 23% reduction in total power at the same speed compared to N2P with NanoFlex. In a separate comparison against baseline N2P, TSMC put A14 at 50% higher energy efficiency, 22% higher drawn transistor density, and 23% higher logic density.

Industry observers note that A14 also gives customers a path to A13. The foundry claims customers can cut die area by about 6% without changes to their A14 design flow. Furthermore, to take even more advantage of A13 and get 5% higher energy efficiency, all the designers have to do is re-engineer the M0 metal layer, reshape OD, and use VT Flex cells (cells that can use different threshold-voltage options for their NMOS and PMOS transistors).

Industry observers note that TSMC expects to start risk production using A14 in the second half of 2027, with mass production following in the second half of 2028. Chief executive C.C. Wei mentioned in October that the firm had already seen more customer activity on A14 than on N2 at a comparable stage of development and expects A14 to become a bigger node than its 2nm-class predecessor. A13 is set to reach the high-volume manufacturing stage in the second half of 2029.

Industry observers note that one of the key parts of the TSMC announcement is the readiness of the 0.9 version of the PDK and the electronic design automation (EDA) tools ecosystem. What matters about v0.9 is that the industry considers this revision ready for design work, which means that customers can start designing chips with confidence that they will meet their performance and power goals. Furthermore, TSMC has validated two complete flows — by Cadence and Synopsys for A14, with Siemens EDA's flow coming later.

"Today, both Cadence and Synopsys have successfully completed full design flow certification for the Cortex-A725," the spokesman said. "This program tests the full chain of implementation and sign-off EDA tools with TSMC foundation IP. We expect it to benefit the entire A14 design community. This table summarizes A14 v0.9 certification for our three major EDA partners, Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens, across automatic placement and routing, library characterization, timing, power, EM/IR, and other sign-off flows. Siemens is targeting Q4 for transistor-level EM/IR certification. So the A14 v0.9 design ecosystem and the PDK are ready for design-in.

Automatic placement and routing (APR).

Electromigration and voltage-drop analysis (EMIR).

Layout-versus-schematic checks and layout parasitic extraction (LVS/LPE).

Resistance and capacitance extraction (RC).

Transistor-level timing analysis.

It has been revealed that as of October 1, Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens EDA all had A14 v0.9-certified tools for design rule checks, dummy fill, layout-versus-schematic verification and layout parasitic extraction (LVS/LPE), resistance and capacitance extraction, and circuit simulation. Cadence and Synopsys also had certified tools for automatic placement and routing, library characterization, timing and power analysis, custom circuit design, and electromigration and voltage-drop (EM/IR) analysis at both the design and transistor levels.

In a recent development, synopsys alone had certified transistor-level timing analysis, which gave it coverage across all 13 categories versus 12 for Cadence and five for Siemens EDA. Cadence and Synopsys also completed full-flow certification on an Arm Cortex-A725 design with TSMC foundation IP, from synthesis and physical implementation through electrical, physical, and thermal sign-off. Siemens EDA's transistor-level EM/IR certification is in progress and is due in Q4 2026.

#138670. Show, Don't Certify: How to Prepare for Your First Data Analyst Job

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1566 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

Show, Don't Certify: How to Prepare for Your First Data Analyst Job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • It has been revealed that getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show.
  • Recent findings suggest that many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

It has been revealed that getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show. This plan breaks preparation into eight skill areas, pairs each one with a learning option and a hands-on task, and gives you a simple test for knowing when to move on.

Recent findings suggest that many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews. Their CVs list SQL, Excel and Tableau, yet nothing on the page demonstrates those tools being used to answer a real question. Recruiters reading dozens of similar applications need something more concrete.

A course can give your learning a sensible order, but a completion badge says little about how you think. A small analysis that states its question, explains its method and admits its limits tells a hiring manager far more. This plan aims to collect that kind of proof while you learn, not after.

Start by collecting ten to twenty entry-level postings in the industry you want to join, and tally the tools and tasks they mention. You will swiftly see a pattern. Some roles are built around Excel and routine reporting, while others want SQL, a BI platform and a bit of Python.

Recent findings suggest that the wider market follows a similar shape. Jobright’s 2026 analysis of data analyst hiring, which looked at 2025–2026 postings from LinkedIn, Indeed and Levels.fyi, found that more than 80% of data analyst jobs mention SQL, over 60% mention Excel or Google Sheets, and roughly half mention Python or R. Let your own tally decide the order you learn in, but expect SQL to sit near the top.

As you work through each area below, finish with something you can show someone: a query, a tidied dataset, a chart, a one-page report or a portfolio project. Free material is often enough if you can stay disciplined. Pay for teaching only when it gives you something you cannot get alone, such as feedback, accountability or a fixed timetable.

SQL is how analysts pull, join and summarise records from a database, and a tool like Tableau lets other people explore what you found. Treat them as one workflow rather than two subjects: frame a question, write the query, sanity-check the numbers and present the result so a non-technical reader can follow it.

Sources indicate that SQLBolt offers free, bite-sized SQL lessons that run in the browser, and Tableau publishes free training videos on connecting to data and building dashboards. Used together, they are enough to produce a small end-to-end project.

If you learn better with a set schedule and an instructor checking your work, you could learn to analyse data with SQL and Tableau from scratch through a guided programme at Heicoders Academy in Singapore. Whichever route you take, compare what is covered, how feedback is given, when sessions run and the full cost against what free resources already offer.

Proof you can show: A working SQL query set and your first published dashboard.

Move on when: You can take a question from idea to dashboard on your own, without following a tutorial line by line.

Sources indicate that spreadsheets are still where much of a team’s day-to-day reporting lives, especially when colleagues don’t write SQL. Get comfortable with filtering, pivot tables, and lookup functions, and learn to spot quiet errors like dates saved as text or one category spelled three different ways.

Recent findings suggest that the next step is automating the cleanup so it doesn’t have to be repeated by hand each month. Microsoft’s Power Query documentation shows how to import and reshape data in recorded steps that refresh when upcoming data arrives. The same ideas apply in other spreadsheet tools too.

Proof you can show: A messy export turned into a summary that refreshes itself.

Move on when: You can clean an untidy CSV and build a report that updates when the source file changes.

Recent findings suggest that for most junior analyst roles, the technical interview is a SQL test. Basic SELECT statements won’t be enough; interviewers like to probe joins, subqueries, common table expressions and window functions, which answer everyday questions such as running totals or each customer’s first purchase.

Practise with timed problem sets and review your answers for correctness as well as speed.

Proof you can show: Confidence going into a live or take-home SQL test.

Move on when: You can solve intermediate problems in around 15 to 20 minutes each without looking up syntax.

According to recent reports, take-home assignments often come with data that has been made messy on purpose. Reviewers want to see how you deal with missing values, duplicates and inconsistent formats, and whether they can follow your reasoning afterwards.

Keep a short cleaning log as you work, noting each change and why you made it. A separate sheet tab or a list of comments in a notebook both work.

Proof you can show: A take-home submission a reviewer can audit step by step.

Move on when: Every change to your dataset is written down with a reason.

Case-study questions test whether you can read numbers sensibly, not just produce them. A working grasp of distributions, means and medians, spread, correlation and sampling will keep you away from the mistakes that undo otherwise good answers, such as quoting an average that a few extreme values have pulled out of shape.

Proof you can show: Clear, careful answers in case-study interviews.

Move on when: You can explain in everyday language why two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

According to recent reports, every chart should help someone answer a specific question. Learn where bars, lines, scatter plots and simple tables each work best, and how axis ranges, labels and colour can nudge a reader towards the wrong conclusion. On a dashboard, the most key finding should be the first thing people see.

According to recent reports, datawrapper’s guidance on picking chart types is a useful free reference. As practice, show the same result in two different chart types and decide which one represents the data more honestly.

Proof you can show: Portfolio charts that make a point, not just show off features.

Move on when: A person who has never seen your data can spot the main finding and its caveat at a glance.

It has been revealed that what counts as a useful metric depends on the role. Marketing analysts focus on conversion and retention, operations analysts on delivery times and capacity, and finance analysts on margins and cash flow. Choose one sector and learn exactly how its key measures are defined.

Proof you can show: A project built around the questions your target industry actually asks.

Move on when: You can define several sector metrics and describe how a manager would use each one.

Your portfolio is where the other seven areas come together. Two or three deep, well-documented projects will say more about you than a long list of quick ones. Give each project a README that sets out the question, the data, your method, the findings and the limitations.

Proof you can show: A portfolio link and a write-up you can talk through in an interview.

Move on when: Every project clearly explains what it asked, how you answered it and what you found.

Sources indicate that there is no need to finish all eight areas before you apply. Once you can use the tools your target roles mention, speak honestly about your work and point to two or three clearly explained projects, start sending applications and keep learning alongside them.

Adjust each application to the job. Lead with a reporting example for spreadsheet-heavy roles, a query that solved a real problem for SQL roles, and a chart that supported a decision for visualisation roles. Be upfront about which work you built independently and which came from guided exercises.

Do I really need eight courses? No. These are skill areas, not eight required qualifications. A single resource can cover several of them, and practice you do on your own counts as much as classroom learning.

Sources indicate that is it possible to prepare using only free material? Yes. Free tutorials, open textbooks, official documentation and public datasets cover the fundamentals well. The harder parts are sticking to a routine and finding people who will give you honest feedback.

Which should come first, SQL or spreadsheets? It depends on the jobs you want. Spreadsheets are an easy starting point for reporting roles, while SQL is expected wherever databases are involved. You will want both eventually, so start with whichever your target postings stress most.

According to recent reports, how many portfolio projects should I have? Two or three solid ones are a good start. Each should show a clear question, steps someone else could repeat and an honest reading of the results, rather than several near-identical dashboards.

According to recent reports, do I need a certificate before I apply? Not usually. Some employers ask for one, but many judge skills through interviews, take-home tasks and tests instead. Go by what each posting actually requires.

#138669. Tech Report: "I'm betting on the sickos" - Signet City looks to 'expand the scope of RPGs' by drawing on the success of Citizen Sleeper

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2531 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: "I'm betting on the sickos" - Signet City looks to 'expand the scope of RPGs' by drawing on the success of Citizen Sleeper

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I last spoke to Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin, it was on the eve of Citizen Sleeper 2's release.
  • "I feel a certain responsibility that comes with success," Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - told me at the time.
  • They wanted the definition of RPGs to be "expanded", to make them as varied as "rich and varied" as tabletop RPGs can be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I last spoke to Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin, it was on the eve of Citizen Sleeper 2's release. Like its predecessor, the game was a critical hit, cementing Damian Martin's reputation as one of the most successful independent game developers around. But they weren't content. They wanted to do more, to push more, to stretch the idea of what a role-playing video game could be.

"I feel a certain responsibility that comes with success," Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - told me at the time. "I feel lots of things about this medium, and I feel if I'm in the one percent of indie developers - and the even smaller percent of solo developers - who manage to make something and have that thing be successful, then I have responsibility towards putting things into the industry and into the world that contribute somehow to whatever I think the industry should be doing.".

They wanted the definition of RPGs to be "expanded", to make them as varied as "rich and varied" as tabletop RPGs can be. Citizen Sleeper was a step towards realising that goal but even it had limitations, which is why Damian Martin has returned to take things a step further with their next game Signet City. Declared during this year's somewhat samey-feeling Summer Game Fest, it's a startlingly original work.

Signet City was enigmatic. Revealed in a cinematic trailer, it was black and white, bleak, thick-lined, smoggy, and dirty; choked in industrial decay and brimming with post-punk non-conformance. It was also first-person, a notable change for Damian Martin, whose games have, up until now, been zoomed out and abstracted. Most eye-catching of all, though, was the descriptor "fungalpunk" - a game in which we'd play as a parasite in someone's mind. As far as expanding the scope of RPGs goes: "100 percent that is exactly what I'm trying to do here," Gareth Damian Martin tells me now.

In a recent development, we talk in a video call in the immediate aftermath of Signet City's announcement - apologies for not writing this until Not-GTA Week, though what an opportunity that presented - and Damian Martin is as calm and eloquent and thoughtful as ever, nestled in a compact office decorated with collages of their current influences. This room looked different when we spoke about Citizen Sleeper 1, looked different when we spoke about Citizen Sleeper 2, and it looks different again now. Damian Martin is a visual person, as someone with a visual design background would be.

Industry observers note that with Signet City only just announced, questions abound. The announcement trailer doesn't reveal much (not much has come out since, either), but we do know it takes place in the North of England in the 80s. It's a setting I'm not sure we've ever had in games, and one that's woefully overlooked in entertainment in general, barring BBC TV shows like Our Friends in the North and Boys from the Blackstuff, which Damian Martin directly references. We know there are themes like industrial decay, welded as they are to that time and place. But there's been no talk of how the game plays, or what being a parasite in someone's mind means.

After speaking with Damian Martin, I've got a much better idea. But first, to the beginning. Signet City is an idea they've had floating around their head for a very long time. This was the game they pitched to their publisher Fellow Traveller after Citizen Sleeper 1 came out, but decided to hold in favour of making Citizen Sleeper 2 - a decision driven partly by a desire "to build myself a bigger platform" to launch a new game idea from. The idea originated in a very unexpected place: the musician Sting. Damian Martin was doing theatre design for Sting's musical show The Last Ship before they became a full-time game-maker (go back even further in Damian Martin's life and you'll find a degree in puppetry there). They had to research Newcastle in the 1980s because of it. The Last Ship is about Sting's upbringing in Wallsend, a town near Newcastle, in the wake of a shipyard being closed there - the town's source of sustenance. And it was while working on the project that the 80s imprinted on Damian Martin's mind.

According to recent reports, "I was looking at these pictures of these massive gleaming ships hanging over the top of little terraced houses," they say, "and this conflict between time periods and ideas of society, and I remember thinking at the time: that was science-fiction somehow. When you look at those images, it could be a spaceship; that ship that's being built in Newcastle might as well be a spaceship, especially science-fiction of the 80s - a lot of it was about that.

Industry observers note that "It just stuck in my brain and I started to work up this fictional 1980s British city that would be in that period of de-industrialisation and social change," they continue. "But would be based on a completely different kind of industrial background and have this weird kind of fungalpunk technology layered into it. So that's been sitting around in my head for almost 10 years slowly accruing material and reference points and things.".

Fungalpunk: there's that word again, but what does it mean? I've heard of cyberpunk and steampunk, not that I could tell you easily what they mean, but I've never heard of fungapunk - I don't think anyone has. Thankfully, in this case, it's fairly literal. "You are fungal in a very true sense," Damian Martin indicates. You are a fungal parasite and there are themes of decay and reinvigoration, things fungi are closely tied to. One of the phrases Damian Martin has been using as a north star for the project - something they do on all of their projects - is the idea of being "a fungal superhero", which makes me giggle. I've definitely not heard that before either.

According to recent reports, it's an idea inspired by a 1989 Japanese film called Tetsuo: The Iron Man - about a salary man who's slowly turning into metal - that Damian Martin adores. "I love it so much," they say. "It's an amazing movie, a beautiful movie, and really strange. And so I wanted to do something that was in that vibe. The way that that film commits to the idea of a body becoming metal and the visceral kind of strangeness of that. I wanted to do something that was about humans and becoming fungal; which we already are, we already have lots of bits of bacteria and fungal nail infections - we are multitudes.".

The punk side of the equation is, again, fairly literal. It refers to the post-punk cultural and musical scene at the time. The scene is often overshadowed by the brasher, more aggressive punk movement, but it's one that's just as anti-establishment, albeit in perhaps in a deeper, darker, more nihilistic way. Think Joy Division referencing novelist JG Ballard in its songs, for example. "Post-punk was this engagement with structural politics and transgressive fiction and all kinds of interesting major ideas getting into pop culture through music," Damian Martin states.

It has been revealed that now watch the game's trailer again; you can feel all these things oozing through it. The aesthetic, the music, the setting. There are also significant clues - although they're not obvious - about how the game plays. We see the start of a character called Sid's story in the trailer, who's one of the hosts we can inhabit in the game. We choose an area of the city we want to play in, then drop into a person's head who lives or operates there. And in Sid's case, she wakes up in a river just as we - the parasite - wake in her mind. Twins!

Recent findings suggest that we control Sid as we would a character in another first-person game - Dishonored or Skyrim are two examples Damian Martin uses - and we see a bit of this in the trailer. What we don't see are any other mechanics, which are, once more, dice rolls related to skills, as in Citizen Sleeper. In order to do something in the world that isn't insignificantly easy, we need to roll a dice and add modifiers to see if we can achieve it.

Sources indicate that "So the way it works is you drop into someone's head for the day. Let's say we drop into this worker's head for the day and we want to get to a certain part of the city, and let's say we need to kick down a door to get there," says Damian Martin. "Well, we're going to have to make this character really angry to get them to kick down that door, so we're going to maybe get them in an argument with some other fellow workers, and maybe we're going to choose to provoke that argument and then they'll get really angry. Then that will have narrative effects, but also it will have mechanical effects in the sense of, like, okay, now we have a modifier that makes physical strength more powerful, so we can do these physical strength actions.".

Sources indicate that skills are tied to a person's emotions, intriguingly, and your job as the parasite is to find things that affect these emotions so you can amplify them and increase your chances of achieving things. Then at the end of the day, all of that emotion gets "extracted out" and becomes a resource you can permanently improve your host's skills with. "So you start to adjust each of your hosts in a direction you think will be helpful for you to do what you need each day in these hub locations," Damian Martin explains. But this has consequences. Push someone towards angry actions and they'll become a more angry person, understandably. "And that will shape their future even when you're no longer controlling them.".

According to recent reports, which begs the question: what exactly does a parasite need to do? What is a parasite's objective in the game? This is an answer Damian Martin isn't quite ready to give, though they do their best to attempt it. "You have your own objectives as a parasite," they say. "You don't have an objective like: this is your mission, parasite. But there are some bigger offers coming to you through your sensorium, through your experience of voices and attractions and tastes and smells, that are leading you in different places as a parasite. That's your objective, to grow and gain power, although to what end you don't initially know.".

It's in this parasitical difference Signet City starts to stand apart. For starters, it's just appealing weird to be a parasite, though as Damian Martin muses, aren't we often parasites in relation to characters in tabletop role-playing games? "We push them around; sometimes we talk for them and sometimes we listen to them; sometimes we use our name and sometimes we use their name." Here, it's simply out in the open. "I wanted to create an RPG where I acknowledged and then also played that into the fiction," they say.

Sources indicate that being in a thing in someone's mind allows a host character autonomy, to a degree, so they can have their own motivations and stories and struggles besides yours. They don't have to be thoughtless mannequins awaiting our direction. Dropping into their minds allows us to drop straight into a tense scenario. "Stories for me that are very exciting in fiction and literature are stories about people who are in it," Damian Martin indicates. "They're in the situation already, they're in the shit, they're having to deal with everything.".

In a recent development, the ability to read their minds also lets us know them more intimately than we know characters in other games, who usually, you know, need to speak to us in order for us to understand them. It also circumvents the need for an NPC to suddenly and unnaturally open up to you about their lives, the first moment they meet you, and to provide you with "a neatly packaged challenge". That's not needed here. "The core relationships of the game are actually between you and your hosts," Damian Martin states.

Sources indicate that there's a layer that exists on top of the character's thoughts where the parasite lives and functions - a layer of feelings and emotions and sensory reactions to a world outside. A hopefully quite bizarre and alien layer, which presents challenges of its own, because how do you describe the experiences of a parasite in someone's mind? "What does it feel like to be a parasite and how do I make that comprehensible to a human?" Damian Martin wonders. They are good questions I can't wait to experience the answers to.

Industry observers note that but when will that be? There's no release date yet, and when we talked in the summer, Signet City was only halfway through development. It was declared early partly to make sure people understood it wasn't Citizen Sleeper 3, and partly because people could probably use some time to sit with the idea for a bit and digest it. "We can't just drop it all on everyone's heads," Damian Martin says, "because I think the potential for it being misunderstood or just ignored is high.".

Sources indicate that and that's a telling admission for a project which has been characterised by Damian Martin multiple times as a risk - as even "the biggest swing I have ever taken". They seemed genuinely nervous about announcing it, though some of those nerves were subsiding by the time we talked. They're not entirely gone, mind you. There's a lingering awareness that Signet City is upcoming and different enough that people might not gel with it, though that's the price of pushing at boundaries, I suppose.

According to recent reports, "What worries me more," Damian Martin notes, "is have I still got it? Am I able to produce things that are appealing and exciting to people just based on my own tastes and obsessions and interests? When it comes to announcing something like Signet City, that's what makes me really nervous - more than industry, more than money, more than anything. Is this actually interesting?".

In a recent development, of course, it's easy for me to say they shouldn't worry. It's exciting when a game blares as loudly and uniquely as Signet City did during Summer Game Fest, though that is obviously no guarantee it'll find an audience. But I think it will. I'm convinced there are more people like me who it will appeal to. Gareth Damian Martin is betting on it. "I'm betting on the sickos," they say. "The thing I've learned is that my obsessions are sticky and they stick to other people, and I think there's something in art where we really like to be tourists in other people's obsessions - that's a fun place to be. That's what I'm hoping for.".

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a latest generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • Sources indicate that A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.
  • Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a latest generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

Sources indicate that A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

Recent findings suggest that the potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," noted Sudbø.

Sources indicate that rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an crucial advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

Sources indicate that skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

Recent findings suggest that in the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

Sources indicate that "For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

It has been revealed that the ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A Newly introduced Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly notable if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

Recent findings suggest that "The findings give us upcoming insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become key for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling upcoming computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, U.S. defense leaders considered invoking a Cold War-era law in an attempt to force the manufacturer to reinstate him, according to a new report. Huang was given his CEO job back earlier this week, with the board reminding the founder of the importance of "candor and honesty" in the future. Now, The Washington Post reports that U.S. officials were so keen to ensure that Huang was reinstated that they brainstormed ideas as to how they could make it happen. One of the options on the table was the Defense Production Act, or DFA, a 1950 law that allows presidents to interfere with private companies. The law is usually used to force those companies to supply the military during wartime, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, wondered whether it could also be used to put pressure on Nvidia's board.

While the DFA doesn't explicitly give the president the power to place a particular person into the CEO role at a company, it could still be wielded to achieve the same result. “Essentially, they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects,” one of three people reportedly familiar with the discussions said. Such a move would have limited Nvidia's ability to sell components for a profit, affecting its production plans and share price as a result.

It has been revealed that the way in which U.S. officials pushed for Huang's return before his November 23 reinstatement is unprecedented. Current U.S. President Donald Trump called for Huang to be given his job back on multiple occasions, including when talking to reporters at the White House. Trump also confirmed that he called into an Nvidia board meeting to pressure members to bring Huang back just 11 days after he resigned. And with Huang still set to face questions from China congressional and Senate Banking committees, Trump has admitted that a pardon for the CEO is "always an option." This came after it was suggested that Huang could plead the Fifth Amendment for fear of incriminating himself and landing himself in legal hot water.

The U.S. military views Nvidia and its advanced AI chips as vital to national security, perhaps explaining why officials have been so keen to ensure Huang's return. Trump and Huang have a strong relationship, with the former joining the president aboard Air Force One for a recent trip to China. This came after Huang was initially snubbed for a trip that also included former Apple CEO Tim Cook and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

#138663. Latest Update: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

Latest Update: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • According to recent reports, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

According to recent reports, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

Recent findings suggest that conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

Recent findings suggest that this unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," claims Egues.

Sources indicate that to minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

Recent findings suggest that the term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

It has been revealed that although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," indicates the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

According to recent reports, the proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Recent findings suggest that superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

It has been revealed that "In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the newly introduced approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

In a recent development, the researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

According to recent reports, "It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

Recent findings suggest that the first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the latest research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

In a recent development, "Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Sources indicate that ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

It has been revealed that "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," notes Egues.

Industry observers note that this behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially notable. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

It has been revealed that this fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

Industry observers note that the approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

According to recent reports, these calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

Industry observers note that the results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

It has been revealed that "All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely upcoming materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

Recent findings suggest that from the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

In a recent development, from a technological perspective, the study demonstrates how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

Anthropic is rolling out a latest Claude app for Android that picks up a Material 3 Expressive redesign.

Confirmed on Twitter/X by Anthropic Product Manager Robert Bye, Claude is now rolling out a Material 3 Expressive redesign for its Android app that, while not a full embrace of Google’s design language, does make a clear attempt to better fit in on Android.

The updated design picks up a bottom-bar UI as opposed to relying fully on the old hamburger menu – it still exists, but it’s mainly for chat history now. You can see M3 elements throughout the app, including in the model switcher and the background of chats. It’s clearly themed to match Anthropic’s aesthetic, and there’s no obvious implementation of Material You colors, but it all fits within the general Material 3 guidelines – much more so than the original app.

The one flaw we spotted was the predictive back implementation, which gets a neat animation to move the search bar but is supposed to show a preview of the previous screen, but that’s just nit-picking, really.

The latest Claude app for Android is rolling out now.

What Is the Best UI design Tool? 8 Tools Compared by the Job They Do (2026)

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your users discover first: broken layouts, usability problems that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your users discover first: broken layouts, usability problems that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that rolls out the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Recent findings suggest that most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:.

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce new violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

Sources indicate that there are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner.

These platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

Chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

Pricing: Free proposal with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and customers. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so initiative coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

In a recent development, percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

In a recent development, strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free initiative includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited customers and projects.

Trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs swiftly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid intends with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

In a recent development, strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Recent findings suggest that trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free proposal, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with big cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

Recent findings suggest that backstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

In a recent development, strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report shows reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

Trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

Sources indicate that test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

Playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Sources indicate that visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an enhancement flag.

Sources indicate that best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Industry observers note that cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that shows the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Sources indicate that visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Sources indicate that visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

According to recent reports, visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a newly introduced framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:.

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change reveals up on the pull request that caused it.

It has been revealed that "Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:.

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

In a recent development, playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

Recent findings suggest that no. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Industry observers note that playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Recent findings suggest that most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states swiftly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.
