📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest York Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a bill that effectively bans the sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots within the state over concerns about what they might say to kids. But the ban will come too late for this Holiday season, leaving parents at risk of buying toys without realizing the risks that they could pose to their children. The ban will come into effect 90 days from Tuesday, November 24, WXXI News reports, and targets toys like stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that use a microphone and speaker to allow children to communicate with a relatively rudimentary chatbot. But with safeguards often lacking, it can be difficult to predict how these toys will behave and what they will say to young children who might not realize what they are speaking to.

Industry observers note that new York's ban comes after similar moves by other states around the United States, with California already announcing a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacturing of AI toys to children under 16. Pennsylvania is also considering similar action. Back in New York, Hochul has hinted that more AI safety proposals are in the works for 2027. “We'll set clear safety standards and put independent experts inside these companies to make sure that they're following the rules, and that we'll insist that humans remain in control, and with aims to contain the danger if something does go wrong,” the governor mentioned. There are a few ways that could happen, with State Senator Andrew Gournardes (D-Brooklyn) noting that a new Common Sense Media Your AI Safety Institute report found AI chatbot toys can undermine a child's relationships with their family and friends.

The ban will hit toy manufacturers, sellers, and operators with fines of $15,000 per day if they are found in violation. It also follows similar tech-focused child safety laws, such as requiring age verification for social media for anyone under the age of 18. Warning labels must also be present. It's possible that Hochul will look to expand that requirement to AI chatbots, including those not built into toys.

Alarm over AI chatbots is nothing latest, of course, but the new wave of devices aimed at children is causing concern. Beyond the impact on children, AI psychosis continues to be an matter, with a June 2025 report finding that OpenAI's ChatGPT encouraged dangerous and untrue beliefs about a range of things, including trying to convince one user that they were Neo from the popular The Matrix movie franchise. Some companies have worked to make their products safer, with limited success. OpenAI released a new version of its ChatGPT chatbot that would be less sycophantic and push back against customers more, only for those users to revolt over the move. OpenAI later rolled the change back.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • USB-C chargers are pretty standardized at this point, but there’s a fun upcoming trend of adding displays to your power brick that I’ve been very much enjoying, and the new PicoGo Pro from Baseus is a great example with three ports, optimized charging, and a cute little character to top it off – and for Black Friday, it’s pretty deeply discounted, too.
  • In a recent development, the Baseus PicoGo Pro (AH22) is a 100W, 3-port USB-C charger designed to top off your laptop, phone, and/or tablet, even all at the same time.
  • Using GaN tech, PicoGo Pro is very compact at about 2 inches tall and a little over an inch wide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

USB-C chargers are pretty standardized at this point, but there’s a fun upcoming trend of adding displays to your power brick that I’ve been very much enjoying, and the new PicoGo Pro from Baseus is a great example with three ports, optimized charging, and a cute little character to top it off – and for Black Friday, it’s pretty deeply discounted, too.

In a recent development, the Baseus PicoGo Pro (AH22) is a 100W, 3-port USB-C charger designed to top off your laptop, phone, and/or tablet, even all at the same time. For anyone who travels often or just has a lot of devices on hand, chargers like this are a must. Having something you don’t have to think twice about when it comes to charging rates is just so nice, and these have come a long way, too.

Using GaN tech, PicoGo Pro is very compact at about 2 inches tall and a little over an inch wide. I remember having single-port chargers that could barely fast-charge my phone that were twice this size just a few years ago. GaN just absolutely rules, and Baseus is using a special version that reduces heat and improves efficiency.

But the two reasons I really like this charger aren’t strictly to do with GaN.

The first is the built-in display. Again, that’s a trend throughout the industry. Anker has several chargers out with built-in displays as the firm helped to really make this popular – the Anker Prime 160W brick is really similar to PicoGo Pro (at a higher price), and it’s the only I’ve been using for months before trying out this Baseus model.

Baseus has a cute little animated character that accompanies your charging, with little eyes when the charger isn’t active and some fun animations to show your charging rate in real-time. Neat! You can “press” the button to move through the UI and even see the specific charging rate of each connected device. You’ll also see that the brick can recognize the device you have plugged in, though Android devices just show a generic “SAMSUNG” or whatever brand you plug in – Anker, again, had a similar set of features in a brick released earlier in 2026, but some of those features were iPhone-only, and that brick was only a 1-port, 45W charger anyway.

Recent findings suggest that but, like that Anker brick, Baseus supports “smart” charging that adjusts to your device. Plugging in a Galaxy Z Fold 8 that was around 65% full, I saw the brick adjust its charging speed to tailor to the phone, initially going up to full speed before settling down around 28W~. You can manually adjust this with “Turbo” or “Gentle” modes, the former maxing out the charging rate and the latter settling in around 15W for a slower charge. That flexibility is great because it means you can adjust the charging rate to what you need in that moment. Full-speed for a quick top-off on a busy day, slower charging overnight to preserve battery health.

Baseus isn’t doing much new here, though the GaN tech mentioned earlier is enhanced by some architecture and algorithm adjustments the company has made behind the scenes, but it’s a really good implementation.

Beyond that, it’s also priced pretty well.

Baseus PicoGo Pro’s full price is $59.99, but you’ll probably rarely see it there. Technically, today is its launch date, and it’s already down by over 30% at $39.70 for Black Friday. Value-wise, this one is hard to beat.

Tech Report: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • But position and time are different.
  • The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Recent findings suggest that understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

Sources indicate that however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

Sources indicate that at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Sources indicate that tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

Recent findings suggest that to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Sources indicate that making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

Sources indicate that to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

Industry observers note that in the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

Industry observers note that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It highlighted that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become vital simultaneously.

In a recent development, for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

Industry observers note that the team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

Sources indicate that raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

Sources indicate that in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

According to recent reports, the findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Industry observers note that transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists newly introduced ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

It has been revealed that "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

In a recent development, the implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

Recent findings suggest that that possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

In a recent development, for Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production concerns that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:.

Industry observers note that start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1. Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

According to recent reports, 2. Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3. Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted consumers hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

Industry observers note that the peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:.

1. Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

According to recent reports, 2. Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

Recent findings suggest that 3. When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4. For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

Industry observers note that 5. On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:.

Industry observers note that 1. Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

In a recent development, 2. Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3. In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

Sources indicate that 4. In the onicecandidate handler, send every newly introduced candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

Industry observers note that one peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

Sources indicate that 1. The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

Sources indicate that 2. The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3. The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

In a recent development, 4. Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

It has been revealed that on a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Recent findings suggest that consumers deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

It has been revealed that listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try upcoming network paths.

In a recent development, use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that indicates every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

Industry observers note that 1. Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2. In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3. Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4. Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

According to recent reports, 5. Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

In a recent development, start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real people arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (444 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models.
  • In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.
  • Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

All-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • Sources indicate that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

Sources indicate that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are right now beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

Industry observers note that in the upcoming system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

It has been revealed that another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Industry observers note that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Recent findings suggest that successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments indicated that the latest architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

It has been revealed that one of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

According to recent reports, however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Recent findings suggest that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

Email remains an important communication channel for web applications. From account verification and password resets to product announcements and customer notifications, many applications depend on email to keep people informed.

For developers, however, implementing email functionality involves more than connecting a service and sending a message. A reliable email system needs to handle authentication, dynamic content, delivery failures, user preferences, event tracking, and integrations with other application components.

Industry observers note that using an email service provider (ESP) can simplify this process. Most modern providers offer REST APIs, SMTP relays, templates, automation features, and reporting tools that developers can integrate into existing applications.

This guide explores the technical considerations involved in building email integrations, including API-based sending, webhook handling, automation workflows, and deliverability.

There are two common ways to connect an application to an email delivery service: SMTP and REST APIs.

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a standard protocol used to transfer email messages between servers. Developers can connect an application to an SMTP server using credentials and configuration settings.

REST APIs provide another approach. Instead of communicating through an email server protocol, an application sends HTTP requests to an endpoint. The provider processes the request and returns a response.

Both methods can support transactional and application-generated emails, but their implementation differs.

An application already supports SMTP configuration.

Developers want a relatively straightforward integration.

Existing frameworks or libraries provide built-in SMTP support.

An application needs programmatic control over email operations.

Developers want structured responses and error handling.

Email functionality needs to integrate with other application services.

The system requires event tracking or additional API capabilities.

The right approach depends on the application's architecture, expected email volume, and integration requirements.

An API integration allows an application to trigger emails in response to specific events.

For example, an ecommerce application might send an order confirmation after a successful payment. A SaaS application could send an account verification message after registration.

A typical integration follows this process:.

The application detects an event.

The backend prepares the recipient and message data.

The backend authenticates with the email provider.

The provider processes the request.

The application records the response and handles any errors.

Consider a Node.js application that needs to trigger an email campaign through an API.

Some platforms, including Mailmodo, provide REST API functionality for triggering campaigns and integrating external applications with email workflows.

The following example demonstrates the general structure of an HTTP request using a campaign-triggering endpoint:.

Sources indicate that this example uses the documented Mailmodo trigger endpoint and request structure. The campaign ID and API key must be replaced with the values from the relevant account.

Notice that the API key is loaded from an environment variable rather than written directly into the source code.

Industry observers note that this is an crucial security practice. Credentials should never be exposed in frontend JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side application bundles.

Recent findings suggest that not every email provider offers the same integration capabilities. Developers should evaluate providers based on their API documentation, authentication methods, supported endpoints, event notifications, and integration flexibility.

For example, Elastic Email provides a REST API that developers can use to send emails and manage different email operations from an application.

According to recent reports, its API uses HTTPS requests and API-key authentication. Developers can use the available endpoints to send messages, manage campaigns, retrieve information, and configure webhook notifications.

When evaluating an email API, consider these technical requirements:.

Authentication: Check how API keys are generated, stored, restricted, and rotated.

Documentation: Look for clear endpoint descriptions, request examples, response formats, and error codes.

SDK availability: Official libraries can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Permission management: Separate credentials for sending emails and accessing account information can reduce unnecessary exposure.

API limitations: Review connection limits, request timeouts, rate limits, and account-level restrictions before deploying an integration.

Recent findings suggest that A provider with extensive features is not necessarily the best option for every project. The crucial consideration is whether its API supports the application's actual requirements.

Sending an email is only one part of the communication process. Applications may also need to know what happens after a message is submitted.

This is where webhooks become useful.

A webhook allows an external service to send an HTTP notification to an application when a particular event occurs.

Depending on the provider, events may include:.

For example, an application could receive a delivery-failure notification and upgrade the corresponding email record in its database.

A basic Express.js webhook endpoint might look like this:.

This is a simplified example rather than a complete provider-specific webhook implementation. A production endpoint should validate the provider's signature or other authentication mechanism and follow its documented payload structure.

In a recent development, it should also handle duplicate events safely. Webhook providers may retry notifications when an application does not respond successfully.

An idempotent event handler prevents the same notification from creating duplicate database updates or triggering repeated actions.

Email automation connects application events with predefined communication sequences.

Instead of manually sending every message, developers can create workflows that respond to user activity.

Consider a SaaS application with the following registration process:.

The backend stores the fresh user.

A verification email is triggered.

If the user does not complete onboarding, a follow-up message may be triggered.

A simplified workflow can be represented as:.

In a production application, email delivery should generally be handled through a background job queue rather than blocking the registration request.

A queue also makes it easier to retry temporary failures, manage sending volume, and prevent email delays from affecting the main application.

Developers should consider tools such as Redis-backed queues or framework-specific job processors when building larger systems.

Industry observers note that automation platforms can also help manage more complex journeys. For instance, a developer can connect application events to an external email workflow instead of implementing every communication sequence independently.

The key is to keep business logic in the application while using the email service to manage message delivery and relevant campaign operations.

A successful API response does not necessarily mean that an email has reached the recipient's inbox.

Email deliverability depends on several technical factors, including domain authentication, sender reputation, message quality, and recipient engagement.

Developers should pay attention to the following configurations.

Sender Policy Framework identifies the mail servers authorized to send messages on behalf of a domain.

A correctly configured SPF record helps receiving servers evaluate whether an email originates from an authorized source.

Sources indicate that domainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages. Receiving servers can use the corresponding public key in DNS to verify the signature.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance builds on SPF and DKIM. It allows domain owners to publish policies for handling messages that fail authentication checks and receive reports about authentication activity.

These three mechanisms should be configured carefully, especially when an application sends emails through multiple providers.

In a recent development, email systems generate useful operational data. However, developers should avoid treating every available metric as an accurate measure of user engagement.

Recent findings suggest that for example, open tracking can be affected by privacy features and automated image loading. Click tracking may also include automated security scans.

More reliable application-level signals can include:.

These events can be connected with email campaign data to understand how communication affects application activity.

Developers should also maintain a clear separation between email delivery records and user account records. This makes it easier to investigate delivery issues without unnecessarily modifying customer data.

When collecting engagement information, applications should follow applicable privacy requirements and respect user communication preferences.

Before deploying an email integration, developers should review the following areas:.

API security: Store credentials in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.

Domain authentication: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

Error handling: Account for failed requests, invalid recipients, and temporary provider errors.

Background processing: Use queues for asynchronous email delivery.

Webhook validation: Verify incoming notifications and handle duplicate events.

Monitoring: Track delivery failures, bounce rates, and application-level outcomes.

Testing: Test email templates across different clients and devices before production deployment.

These practices help create an email system that is easier to maintain, troubleshoot, and scale.

Email integration is an crucial part of modern application development, but a reliable implementation requires more than connecting an SMTP server or calling an API endpoint.

Developers need to consider authentication, asynchronous processing, webhook security, automation logic, domain configuration, and event monitoring.

According to recent reports, REST APIs are useful for applications that need programmatic control over email operations, while SMTP remains a practical option for systems that already support standard mail-server connections. Webhooks add another layer by allowing applications to respond to delivery events and upgrade their internal records.

By choosing an integration method that fits the application architecture and following sound security and deliverability practices, developers can build email functionality that supports both immediate communication needs and long-term application growth.

Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • Industry observers note that the approach has already revealed latest candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

Industry observers note that the approach has already revealed latest candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

In a recent development, this capability could help advance technologies that are vital to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Sources indicate that finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

It has been revealed that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

According to recent reports, the latest technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Newly introduced Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

According to recent reports, light plays an notable role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Sources indicate that much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

It has been revealed that the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

Industry observers note that these differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Sources indicate that beyond identifying latest candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

According to recent reports, the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

Industry observers note that "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he stated. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

Solo developer vibe codes a gallery hosting 36 classic GPU demos

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once upon a time, graphics chip vendors made small applications to demonstrate the power of their fresh hardware.
  • It's hard to appreciate from a modern perspective, but in the early 1990s, high-end real-time 3D graphics were largely the domain of specialized workstations costing tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars.
  • So what's the simplest way to prove your hardware can do what you say it can?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once upon a time, graphics chip vendors made small applications to demonstrate the power of their fresh hardware. The most accessible were those from 3dfx, ATI Technologies, NVIDIA, and Matrox, since these were the companies dominating PC graphics at the time. If you're nostalgic for that era, you've got to check out this GPU Demo Gallery, because the enterprising creator Archit 'arkits' Khode has ported 36 classic PC graphics card demos to the web, and you can view them right in your browser.

It's hard to appreciate from a modern perspective, but in the early 1990s, high-end real-time 3D graphics were largely the domain of specialized workstations costing tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars. By the middle of the decade, companies like 3dfx, Rendition, and VideoLogic (known for PowerVR) were promising to bring hardware-accelerated 3D graphics with filtered textures to ordinary PCs at interactive frame rates for a few hundred bucks. It was honestly hard to believe.

So what's the simplest way to prove your hardware can do what you say it can? Make a demo and actually show it running in person on your hardware. Developing a full game takes a tremendous amount of time, money, and expertise, but a focused tech demo can concentrate on a particular feature or rendering technique and show it off without needing all the systems that make a game playable. And so the GPU tech demo was born.

Industry observers note that "Demos" have a long culture going back way before the 3D accelerator. The "demo scene" (now often written as one word, 'demoscene') goes back to the mid 1980s, the Commodore 64 and the 16-bit micro era, particularly on the Amiga and Atari ST. There's not much of a direct cultural connection between the demoscene and commercial GPU tech demos, but there was some overlap in the talent involved; NVIDIA, for example, had demoscene veterans on its demo team, including programmer Hubert 'Sigfrid' Nguyen of Impact Studios.

The demos in the gallery start from the earliest 3dfx Voodoo demos like 'Demoroom' and 'Flip' and go up through the NVIDIA 'Box of Smoke' demo meant to show off GPU-accelerated computational fluid dynamics. There are some other rough edges; the site has the unmistakable feel of a vibe-coded project, and some of the shortcomings show through in the demos themselves.

Recent findings suggest that the famous NVIDIA Wolfman demo for the GeForce 4 Ti cards lacks its fur (which was the point of the demo), the 3dfx Valley of Ra demo doesn't render correctly (and the controls don't work), and the Toy Soldiers demo is missing all specularity. Also, as Hacker News commenter Narishma points out, most of these demos should be compatible with WebGL1, yet they all require WebGL2 or WebGPU support.

It has been revealed that beyond that, there are a number of key demos missing that I'd like to see added, although the owner of the site is working fast with the help of Claude. When I first checked the site yesterday afternoon, there were only 26 demos, and the most glaring omission was the famous NVIDIA 'Dawn' demo for the GeForce FX GPUs. The lovely sprite is there now, as is ATI's incredible 'Pipe Dream' demo for the R300 (Radeon 9700/9800) family.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Hopefully, arkits can get the errors in the demos cleaned up, and it would be cool to see some classic graphics demos from other vendors implemented. Personally, I'd love to see the DICE-created Matrox EMBM demo and the PowerVR Kyro Energy and Still Life demos, as well as the impressive Dolphins demo for the original Xbox. The early G-SYNC Pendulum and Freesync Windmill demos would be cool, too. Still, even in its current state, arkits' gallery is a wonderful preservation effort for a tiny world that only a handful of people even remember.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alongside a teaser for the upcoming Ear (note) recorder, Nothing CEO Carl Pei has confirmed the firm’s plans for a big 2027 in terms of smartphone releases, as well as a focus on the US market.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Carl Pei says that Nothing right now has “tens of millions of devices in use,” and that there are big aims for 2027.

Industry observers note that this includes “more attention” to the US market for Nothing, with the US being Nothing’s fastest-growing market for audio devices. In 2026, Nothing launched its Ear (3a) earbuds, multiple CMF-branded devices, and two pairs of over-ear headphones including its high-end Headphone (1) Pro in September, all of which are sold in the US (and on sale during Black Friday).

According to recent reports, pei further remarked that Nothing would have a more “aggressive” smartphone release schedule in 2027. Previously, it was said that Nothing would launch six upcoming smartphones next year, following just three new smartphones in 2026.

In a recent development, pei said Nothing now has “tens of millions of devices in use” across its smartphones, earbuds and other products. The organization is also planning to devote more attention to the US market, while pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.

The tech giant noted it has generated more than $2 billion in revenue since its first product release in 2022 and that the US is its fastest growing market for audio gear.

Nothing doesn’t have a strict schedule for newly introduced product rolls out, but Nothing Phone (4a) debuted in March 2026, with Phone (3) launching in the Summer of the year prior. With six new devices supposedly in the works, it’s anyone’s guess as to when they might release.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Your accessibility check in CI is green. axe-core ran, zero violations, and the badge in the README looks great. Your site can still fail WCAG 2.2.

That isn't a bug in axe. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. It added nine success criteria and dropped one (4.1.1 Parsing), and most of the new ones can't be judged by reading the DOM. Deque noted as much when it shipped the first WCAG 2.2 support in axe-core 4.5: the target-size rule would probably be the only new-criterion rule they added, because the others can't be automated without a lot of false positives.

So the rest is on you. This article covers the one criterion axe can check and three it can't (focus not obscured, dragging movements, accessible authentication), with Playwright tests you can drop into a project. I ran all of them against a small test page that fails every criterion on purpose, and against a fixed version of the same page. If you want a plain-language rundown of every change first, WCAG 2.2 vs 2.1 goes through them. Here I only care about what you can put in a pipeline.

Level A and AA are what most contracts and laws point at, so those are the ones that matter first. The AAA criteria are still worth knowing about.

It has been revealed that that's four AA criteria with something you can script, one of which axe already handles. The rest of this article goes through those four.

Recent findings suggest that the AA rule is smaller than most people expect: a pointer target should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or sit far enough from its neighbours that a 24px circle centred on it wouldn't overlap another target or that target's own circle. There are exceptions, including inline links in a sentence, and targets whose size the browser controls.

Recent findings suggest that axe-core has a target-size rule for this. One catch: it isn't part of a default run. In my setup (axe-core 4.14.1 through @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0), a plain analyze() on the broken page reported nothing at all. The rule only revealed up once I asked for it:.

It has been revealed that on the broken page this lists the three 16px toolbar buttons by selector. On the fixed page, with 32px buttons, it passes. If you've been running axe for years and never seen a target-size result, this is why.

Industry observers note that some context on how common the problem is. In the scan data behind my last SitePoint article, 34.5% of the 1,025 sites had controls below a stricter 44px threshold. That is a tougher standard than the 24px that AA asks for, so don't read it as "a third of sites fail 2.5.8". Plenty of those would pass. But it does show how many production sites ship tiny controls.

If you'd like a quick look at one page before wiring anything up, browser tools such as axe DevTools, WAVE, or a WCAG checker will show the same thing.

It has been revealed that axe can't test it, because you have to press Tab and look at where the browser scrolled. Two details caught me out building this:.

The check below samples a grid of points inside the visible part of the focused element and asks the browser what's on top at each one. If none of the points land on the element or its children, it's covered.

On my broken page it reported nine hits: links hidden behind the footer going forward ("Section 4 link", "Section 10 link", "Section 16 link") and the toolbar buttons and a few links hidden behind the header coming back. The output names the element and the key, which is what you want when you're staring at a failed build.

The fix is one CSS rule, sized to your sticky elements:.

That tells the browser to leave room when it scrolls a focused element into view. With it in place the same test passes.

Industry observers note that be aware of what this can't see: a modal that opens over the page, or a chat widget that only appears after a delay, will not show up unless your test opens or waits for them. Adrian Roselli's piece on 2.4.11 and adversarial conformance is worth reading for the awkward cases.

Anything you can do by dragging needs a way to do it with a single click or tap, unless dragging is essential. Sortable lists, sliders, kanban cards, file reorderers: all of them.

According to recent reports, you can't prove a drag alternative works from a script. But you can catch the obvious mistake, which is a draggable item with no button anywhere near it:.

The limit is real. It only recognises the native draggable attribute. Libraries built on pointer events, such as dnd-kit, don't set it, so this test will walk right past them. If you use one of those, replace the selector with whatever your component renders, or add a test per drag component. Treat it as a tripwire for the common case, not a verdict.

The fix, in the fixed page, is a pair of "Move up" and "Move down" buttons on each item, each with an accessible name that claims which item it moves.

Sources indicate that this dispatches a synthetic paste event and checks whether anything called preventDefault() on it. It catches the old onpaste="return false" trick, and it catches script-based blockers too. It does not tell you whether your login has a CAPTCHA that needs an alternative, or an emailed one-time code you must retype. Those need a person.

On a pull request, a plain GitHub Actions job is enough:.

Point PAGE_URL at a running preview, and run the tests against the pages that matter most: sign-in, checkout, anything with a sticky element. Don't try to crawl everything on the first pass. A test that fails for reasons nobody owns gets deleted within a month.

Four things I haven't tried to automate, and wouldn't:.

It has been revealed that automation will keep the regressions out. It won't tell you the work is finished. A green build and a conformant site are different things, and WCAG 2.2 widened the gap between them.

The tests and both test pages are small enough to read in one sitting. Copy what's useful, change the selectors, and keep the broken page around: it's a handy way to check that a test fails when it should.

Industry observers note that about the author: [name] builds WCAGsafe, an accessibility scanner. The study data above comes from its scans; the code in this article is independent of it and runs against any page.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that good morning. Today I’m deciding whether the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer passes the “people just standing around” test, trying the new Material 3 Expressive Claude app on my Android devices, and stocking up on discounted XTEINK e-readers for Christmas gifts.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous complications here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

According to recent reports, eleven days after leaving Nvidia, Jensen Huang is back as president, CEO, and a board director. The board voted unanimously to reinstate him on Monday, saying it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead following a series of meetings. It also noted input from senior levels of the US government left it confident that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

I didn’t see this coming. Huang was dishonest to the public and to his board. He admitted to having affairs not only with an alleged Chinese spy, but also with an employee who directly reported to him. He is accused of facilitating the sale of Nvidia AI chips to companies like Megaspeed that knowingly purchased them with the intention of smuggling them into China, a contravention of US trade restrictions.

In a recent development, as recently as November 17th, the board chair, Harvey Jones, reiterated that the manufacturer had no intention of bringing back Huang as CEO. But things changed quickly on Sunday as President Trump reportedly reassured the board that Huang’s reinstatement posed no security risk to US intelligence, something that the new Democratic-led Congress will be sure to test via repeated subpoenas in the new year.

As Huang walked into the atrium at Nvidia’s headquarters, staff gathered around to cheer his return, and he addressed the crowd by saying he would be a “better CEO the second time around,” as if 11 days of unemployment had given him sufficient time to evaluate his past behavior.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s stock was up over 30% on Monday, rebounding from a disastrous end to last week that wiped out $4 trillion in Nasdaq value. It’s hard not to see Huang’s return as a direct response to this short-term disruption, which also hinted at a much more serious correction in the stock market. Nvidia’s stock had already fallen 24% between the day Huang resigned and Friday’s crunch, and with looming regulation from Congress in 2027, a rudderless AI industry could have been disastrous for the US economy writ large.

Sources indicate that though things may appear to be back to normal, or as normal as possible given the insanity of the past couple of weeks, Huang has returned to a very different trade environment. While he was away, Nvidia’s board formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to investigate whether the firm’s actions violated any US embargoes. And as part of Huang’s return, Nvidia has committed to hiring its first chief compliance officer, an executive who will ostensibly not report directly to the CEO.

I was pretty gobsmacked when I saw the news of Huang’s return come across the wire at 9am ET yesterday. I’m still wrapping my head around it. Is Nvidia too substantial to fail, or just a symptom of a larger interdependency between the US executive branch and Big Tech? Huang promises to be a better leader this time around, but to whom: his employees, his customers, or his shareholders? Because he appears to be a very different person to each of those groups.

In a recent development, better-tasting water for your morning coffee, everyday cooking, or a house full of holiday guests? Waterdrop Filter’s Black Friday sale has options for all three, from high-capacity under-sink reverse osmosis systems to installation-free countertop models. Upgrade your kitchen with the X12 under-sink system for $899, save space with the compact G6A6 for $189.99, or skip the plumbing with the M6HG countertop system for $299, which delivers filtered hot water for coffee and tea in seconds.

In a recent development, whichever setup fits your routine, use code 9TO5GBF26 to take an extra 5% off those sale prices. Waterdrop’s offers also extend to whole-home filtration and replacement refrigerator filters, giving you plenty of ways to upgrade without stretching your holiday budget. Shop Waterdrop’s Black Friday deals on Amazon before the sale ends November 30th.

Since it’s Black Friday week, I figured I’d round up some of the best deals we’ve found so far.

Industry observers note that A discounted Pixel: The Pixel 10 at $600 is a really good deal. Recent software updates have closed some of the feature gaps with the Pixel 11, and the hardware is still solid even a year after launch. If you want better cameras, the Pixel 11 Pro at $749 is an absolute steal.

Recent findings suggest that the gaming-tablet deal: The Legion Tab Gen 5 at $599 makes much more sense than it did at $899: an 8.8-inch 165Hz display, a 12GB/256GB configuration, and an included folio. It’s a good fit for someone specifically seeking a compact Android gaming machine.

The last-generation watch: The 40mm Galaxy Watch 8 at $199 is the sort of older smartwatch worth considering when annual upgrades are modest. And because the Watch 9 is basically identical, I’d go for the Watch 8. If you are looking at Samsung’s latest and greatest, the Galaxy Watch 9 is $379 with a free $50 Amazon gift card, which is a decent deal, too.

It has been revealed that A deal on the year’s best Android foldable: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is showing up at $1,499.99 for some lucky shoppers and $1,549.99 for the rest. Either way, it’s Samsung’s best product of 2026, and my current favorite gadget.

Some more great Black Friday deals:.

It has been revealed that google’s latest mid-sized sedan AI model is taking the world by storm. Gemini 4 Neon is technically the middle sibling in Google’s lineup, with Carbon at the top and Hydrogen at the bottom, but everyone seems to agree it absolutely cooks.

It has been revealed that if you’ve spent any time on X over the past few days (I hate myself for writing that), you’ll likely have seen an uptick in fervor over Google’s latest model, which seems to outperform Claude Opus 5.5, and even Gemini 4 Carbon itself, in many benchmarks and real-world tests. Even Google is providing some helpful guidance about when to use one or the other.

One thing I’ve read again and again about Neon is how adept it is at writing. I’m of two minds about this: the better an AI gets at doing my job, the less necessary I am at mentioned job. On the other hand, I’m so tired of obvious AI slop that a model that actually writes well sounds like a relief. At least when I’m unemployed, I won’t be yelling at the screen all day about why the robot yet again used negative parallelism.

In a recent development, I didn’t get to play much GTA VI over the weekend, but I know a few (million) people who did. Publisher Take-Two notes the game generated $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales. That’s an incredible number in any industry, but a truly mind-blowing one in the video game world. Rockstar also released its first patch for the game on Monday to fix a modest number of bugs with the launch code.

In a recent development, if you follow open-weight AI models, you’ll likely have heard of how influential Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 was when it launched in June. Now the manufacturer has released GLM-5.4, and it’s novel as much for its architecture as it is for its benchmarks.

It has been revealed that its Loop Transformer reuses a block of layers to do more computation without adding parameters. The firm is pitching applications beyond software, including games, visual work, and CAD. The 750-million-parameter model reportedly performs at the level of a 2-3 trillion parameter non-looping equivalent, but we’re still waiting on a broader release for real-world testing.

In browser news, Ladybird’s first public alpha is now downloadable for macOS and Linux. It’s built with a brand-newly introduced engine that eschews many of the legacy decisions made by Google’s Chromium team. And the project has the backing of significant names like Shopify, Cloudflare, and Proton. It’s still pretty rough, and features are paltry, but any new competition in the browser space is a win in my book.

  • This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:.
  • Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the upcoming XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.

This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:.

Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the upcoming XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?", and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

Driving for Thanksgiving? These are the worst times to be on the road this week
